summary: Year 6 geometry consolidating three angle configurations: angles at a point (sum 360°), angles on a straight line (sum 180°), and the new element — vertically opposite angles (equal). The pedagogical crux is holding TWO relationships apart on one intersecting-lines diagram: the opposite pair is EQUAL, while each adjacent pair (on a straight line) is SUPPLEMENTARY (sums to 180°). The signature task is 'given one angle, find and justify every other angle', naming the rule used each time. Deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule (both angles equal 180° minus the shared neighbour) is preferred to memorising it as a separate fact. Orientation should be varied — tilted intersections — so 'vertically opposite' is understood as two angles opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not as up-and-down.
misconceptions: Confuses the two relationships — applies the straight-line 180° rule to the opposite pair, giving the vertically opposite angle as 180° minus the known angle instead of equal to it.
Over-generalises 'opposite angles are equal' to conclude all four angles at the intersection are equal, ignoring the supplementary straight-line pairs.
Attaches 'vertically opposite' to up–down orientation, so fails to recognise the opposite pair when the lines are tilted, or mislabels which angles are opposite.
Carries over the wrong whole — uses 180° for angles at a point (or 360° on a straight line).

activities.title: Crossing-lines reasoner: watch the opposite pair stay equal
steps: Work with two straight lines crossing at a point, with all four angles labelled.

Rotate one line and observe how all four angle values change together: each pair of vertically opposite angles grows and shrinks TOGETHER and stays equal, while each adjacent angle changes so that the two angles on each straight line always sum to 180°.
Set the crossing angle to several values and each time read off the opposite pair, confirming it matches the given angle exactly (not 180° minus it).

Deliberately predict what the angle opposite a 130° angle will be; set the crossing angle to 130° and check the opposite angle reads exactly 130° rather than 50°, then rotate and check the opposite angle keeps matching the changing angle.

Repeat with the whole figure tilted so neither line is horizontal or vertical, confirming the opposite pair is still identified as the two angles opposite each other across the vertex, sharing no arm.
activities.insight: As an intersection turns, vertically opposite angles stay equal while each adjacent pair stays supplementary — these are two different claims about the same diagram, and 'vertically opposite' means opposite each other across the shared vertex (sharing no arm), not pointing up-and-down.

activities.title: Given one angle, find and justify the rest
steps: On a tilted intersection with one angle marked (e.g. 43°), work out each of the other three angles.

For EACH angle, state both the value AND the rule that justifies it — e.g. 'this angle is 43° BECAUSE vertically opposite angles are equal' or 'this angle is 137° BECAUSE angles on a straight line sum to 180°'.
Repeat with a different given angle (e.g. 130°, giving an opposite angle of 130° and adjacent angles of 50° each).
Switch to an angles-at-a-point diagram: given two angles (e.g. 150° and 90°) find the unknown as 360 − (150 + 90) = 120°, naming the 360° whole.
Write down every equation you can for an intersection diagram, surfacing both the equal pairs and the two 180° straight lines.
activities.insight: Every unknown angle at an intersection or point can be deduced and JUSTIFIED from a named rule, and the correct 'whole' must be chosen — 360° at a point, 180° on a straight line.

activities.title: Sort angle pairs: equal or supplementary
steps: Look at a crossing-lines diagram with the four angles labelled and sort each pair of angles into 'vertically opposite — equal' or 'adjacent (straight line) — supplementary'.
Answer which rule applies to a specifically named pair, choosing between 'equal' and 'sums to 180°'.
Fill in the value of each unknown angle, resisting the tempting '180 − known' value when the angle is actually the opposite (equal) one.
Try a tilted-intersection item where orientation cannot be used to guess, and a point-diagram item that uses the 360° whole.
Explain WHY vertically opposite angles are equal: both equal 180° minus their shared straight-line neighbour, so they equal each other.
activities.insight: Classifying each pair by its relationship — and deriving 'opposite = equal' from the straight-line rule — cements that the two claims are distinct and reasoned, not interchangeable.

activities.title: Tap-to-reveal angle relationships (vocabulary scaffold)
steps: On a static crossing-lines diagram, tap an angle to reveal its vertically opposite partner (equal) and its two straight-line (adjacent) partners (each supplementary to it).
Use a 'given 130°, what are the other three?' reveal: predict each value and its rule, then lift the flap to check (opposite 130°, adjacent 50° each).
Name each revealed pair aloud with its rule before moving on.
activities.insight: Seeds the vocabulary — 'vertically opposite' vs 'adjacent/straight-line' — and the paired structure of an intersection.

checkQuestion: Draw two straight lines crossing at a point, TILTED so neither line is horizontal or vertical, and mark just one of the four angles as 130°. Say: 'Find the other three angles, and tell me how you know each one.' Then show a second diagram — angles round a point marked 150°, 90° and an unknown — and ask for the unknown. Watch which rule they use for each angle and whether tilt throws them; do not prompt.
checkAnswer: At the intersection: the angle vertically opposite the 130° is 130° (vertically opposite angles are equal); the two adjacent angles are each 50° (angles on a straight line sum to 180°, 180−130). At the point: unknown = 360 − (150+90) = 120°. Justifies each with the correct named rule and is not misled by the tilt.
